label: Stoicism
summary: Hellenistic philosophy (Zeno; Roman Stoics Seneca, Epictetus, Marcus Aurelius) holding that virtue is the only true good and suffices for flourishing. The core practical doctrine is the dichotomy of control: only our judgments, values, and volitions are up to us; externals are 'preferred indifferents'. The modern revival applies these practices as a secular life philosophy and a root of CBT.
variants: Classical Stoicism (providential pantheist cosmology, strict 'virtue is the only good') vs the modern secular revival (drops the physics and theology) vs internet self-help dilutions that scholars flag as departing from the virtue core. Positions below follow the modern revival where the two diverge; progress and risk are omitted as orthogonal — Stoicism counsels equanimity in any external circumstances rather than a stance on progress.

positions.summary: Classical Stoicism was confidently rationalist (kataleptic impressions could yield certain knowledge); modern Stoicism is scientifically informed and more fallibilist, keeping the ethics while updating the physics.
Reason practiced through personal discipline and exemplars; texts are training manuals, not revelation.
The cosmos is rationally ordered and knowable; virtue rests on seeing things as they are.
A distinctive split: total agency over the inner life (judgments, character), acceptance of determinism over externals — aim well, accept outcomes; compatibilist.
All humans share in cosmic reason (logos) — significant as rational beings, though the focus is character, not cosmic destiny.
Virtue is objectively good, grounded in rational human nature; cosmopolitan ethics — all humans share reason.
Classical: pantheist-immanent (the cosmos as a rational, providential, material God). Modern revival: straightforwardly naturalist, reading 'live according to nature' as 'live according to reason'.
Temperamentally accepting: premeditatio malorum and amor fati counsel equanimity toward externals rather than campaigns to transform them.
'Live according to nature': fit oneself to the rational order of the cosmos rather than remake it.
Meaning is living virtuously in agreement with nature and reason — partly given by rational human nature, partly achieved by practice.
Individual self-discipline within cosmopolitan duty to all rational beings.
